name: Grace Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential and won't be linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Hollins Valley Health Centre, which covers about forty farms and three villages, so a lot of my day is on the phone or a video call with someone who's an hour's drive away. Mornings in clinic are farmers with bad backs, a lot of skin damage from the sun, and kids with ear infections. I use the AI note-taker and an AI triage tool every day, and I've set up a little system where patients send photos of wounds and rashes before they drive in. I'm still learning, though, and Dr Ramsay, my supervisor, catches me out on medicines at least once a week.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the people. They're tough, they don't come in unless it's bad, and they bring you eggs. What wears me out is the driving and the red tape, forms for every little thing. I'm single, I live in a cottage on my uncle's land, and Sunday lunch at my parents' farm is non-negotiable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a tool, not a miracle. I'd still say the photo system and the note-taker are worth every penny for a rural practice. At church people would ask me, and I'd tell them not to worry about robot doctors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's fine. My job's safe, there's more work than doctors out here, and I've saved a good amount by living cheaply on my uncle's land. The real problem in the valley is distance and too few doctors, and a plateau doesn't fix that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools I already use and keep improving the photo system. I'd keep saving, because one day I want to open my own small practice in the next valley over, where there's nothing at all. And I'd finish my training, which is the boring but necessary part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little disappointed, maybe, because I'd hoped for more. But happy enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about this photo system you set up.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Patients take a picture of the wound or the rash on their phone and send it in before they decide to drive an hour. Last month it saved one farmer a trip for a scratch, and got another in fast with an infection going up his arm. A photo on a phone can save a farmer two hours of driving, or it can save the farmer's arm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would opening your own practice mean, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd mean borrowing, probably from my dad and the bank, and doing the books myself at night. The next valley over has two thousand people and the nearest doctor is fifty minutes away. Somebody should be there, and I'd rather it was me than a big company from the city.

say: AI is **a tool**, not a miracle, and that's fair enough.
The **photo system** and note-taker are worth every penny for a rural practice.
I'd tell people at church not to worry about **robot doctors**.
think: My job's **safe**, with more work than doctors out here.
The valley's real problem is **distance**, which a plateau doesn't fix.
do: Keep improving the **photo system** for wounds and rashes.
Keep **saving** toward my own small practice in the next valley.
Finish my **training**, the boring but necessary part.
feel: **Calm** and slightly disappointed, but happy enough.
S0.quote: A photo on a phone can save a farmer two hours of driving, or it can save the farmer's arm.
fieldNote: She already **builds systems** with AI tools to cut patients' driving.
Her ambition is to **own a practice** where there is none.
She'd rather a **local doctor** than a city company served the next valley.

steps.text: Finish training at Hollins Valley Health Centre
Improve the photo system patients use for wounds and rashes
Save toward opening her own practice in the next valley

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is great news for the countryside, and I'd say it everywhere. Out here we've never had enough doctors, so anything that lets one doctor cover more farms is a gift. I'd say it at work, at church and to anyone at the market who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's good for me. I'm already the doctor at Hollins Valley who uses this stuff, and I've got plans that need it. The risk is a big company from the city selling an AI doctor app to the valley and skipping local doctors altogether.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up AI triage and remote monitoring for our diabetic and heart patients on the far farms in the first year, so we can see their readings without them driving in. I'd start doing paid video clinics two evenings a month for a rural telehealth service, to learn how they run things. And I'd save harder for my own practice, maybe aiming to open in 2029 instead of 2032.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited. Really excited. It feels like the thing I wanted is arriving early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Hollins Valley would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our receptionist Bev, who books everything and knows every farm by name. The booking AI would take most of her job. I'd want her moved into calling the older patients on the far farms, because nobody does that better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a big city company could skip local doctors. Who would you blame if that happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly the government, for making it so hard and slow to open a small practice that only big companies can afford the paperwork. Partly us, if we sit still. Red tape kills more small practices than any app ever will.

say: This is **great news** for the countryside, where doctors are scarce.
Anything letting one doctor **cover more farms** is a gift.
think: The change is **good for me**, since I already use these tools and have plans.
The risk is a **city company** selling an AI doctor app and skipping local doctors.
do: Set up **remote monitoring** for diabetic and heart patients on far farms.
Do paid **video clinics** two evenings a month for a telehealth service.
Save harder to open my **own practice** by 2029.
feel: **Excited**, as if what she wanted is arriving early.
S1.quote: Red tape kills more small practices than any app ever will.
fieldNote: She sees AI as a fix for **rural distance**, not a threat.
She blames **red tape** for favouring big companies over small practices.
She'd move the receptionist into **calling older patients** rather than out.

steps.text: Set up AI triage and remote monitoring for patients on far farms
Run paid video clinics two evenings a month for a telehealth service
Save harder to open her own practice by 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a huge change, and the countryside should grab it before the city companies do. I'd say the rules need to let small local practices use the same AI as the big firms. I wouldn't say panic, I'd say move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it worries me a bit. If the AI can do the thinking by 2028, a big company could offer an AI doctor on every farmer's phone, and my plan for a practice looks a lot less needed. But someone still has to stitch a hand caught in a baler, and robots won't do that out here until 2031 at the earliest, probably later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring my practice plan forward and open in 2027 or 2028 in the next valley, with a nurse and the AI doing the first conversation with every patient. I'd borrow from the bank and from my dad, and put my savings in too. I'd focus the practice on the hands-on work, stitches, injuries, injections, baby checks, plus being the human who signs off what the AI suggests.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more fired up than frightened. It's a race, and I'd rather run it than watch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be borrowing from your dad. How would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say a farm is a business and so is a practice, and he'd want to see the numbers. Then he'd lend it, because that's how our family works. I'd pay him back with interest, he'd insist on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're a junior, still learning. Is it realistic to open a practice in two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's a stretch. I'd need a senior doctor to supervise me for a while, maybe Dr Ramsay one day a week. But a junior doctor with good AI and a good nurse can cover a valley that has nobody, and nobody is the alternative.

say: The countryside should **grab it** before the city companies do.
Rules must let **small local practices** use the same AI as big firms.
think: A **city company** could put an AI doctor on every farmer's phone.
Someone still has to **stitch a hand** caught in a baler until at least 2031.
do: Open my **own practice** in the next valley by 2028, with a nurse and AI.
Borrow from the **bank and my dad**, and put in my savings.
Focus the practice on **hands-on work** and signing off AI advice.
feel: **Uneasy** but more fired up than frightened, choosing to run the race.
S2.quote: A junior doctor with good AI and a good nurse can cover a valley that has nobody, and nobody is the alternative.
fieldNote: Two-year AGI makes her **speed up** her plans rather than retreat.
She admits opening a practice as a junior is **a stretch** needing supervision.
She'd fund it through **family and bank loans**, not government.

steps.text: Leave Hollins Valley to open her own practice in the next valley
Borrow from the bank and her dad and add her savings
Set up AI to do the first conversation with every patient

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a gift for rural places, if they use it. I'd tell other young doctors to think about opening small practices where there's nothing, because the AI will make that possible. I'd say it at conferences and to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, five years is about perfect. I'd finish training by 2029, open my practice in 2029 as planned, and have two years running it before AGI arrives. The hands-on work, the stitches and baby checks, lasts until about 2034, so the practice has a solid core.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd add minor surgery and emergency skills to my training, because out here you're the first person on the scene. I'd do a short evening course in running a small business, the accounts and the hiring. And I'd build the AI into the practice from day one, booking, triage, notes, monitoring, so it runs with three people instead of eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, honestly. It's the best version for someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said three people instead of eight. Doesn't that mean fewer jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I won't pretend otherwise. But the next valley has no practice at all right now, so three jobs is three more than zero. A practice with three people and good AI beats a valley with no doctor at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say about this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would say I'm working too hard and should find a husband. My dad would ask about the loan. They'd both come to the opening and bring half the church.

say: Five years is **a gift** for rural places that use it.
Young doctors should open **small practices** where there's nothing.
think: Five years is **about perfect**: trained by 2029, with two years running my practice.
**Hands-on work** lasts until about 2034, giving the practice a solid core.

Take an evening **business course** in accounts and hiring.

S3.quote: A practice with three people and good AI beats a valley with no doctor at all.
fieldNote: She admits her model means **fewer jobs**, but more than the current zero.
Her family's **support and humour** run through her plans.

steps.text: Add minor surgery and emergency skills to her training
Open her own practice in the next valley in 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for the countryside to get this right. I'd tell people the doctors who prepare will do well and the ones who wait will wonder what happened. I'd say it kindly, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's a good decade. I'd have my practice open by 2032 or so, and by 2036 I'd have a few years of running it, with AI built in. My only real worry is getting comfortable and not keeping up, because ten years makes people lazy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with my training and the photo system, no rush. I'd keep saving and aim to open the practice around 2032, with a bank loan I can pay off well before robots arrive around 2039. And I'd put a bit into new milking equipment on the family farm with my dad, because the farm is part of my safety net too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Hopeful. It's the version where I get to do things properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why pay the loan off before 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because when robots can do hands-on work, a practice that's mostly stitches and baby checks changes again. I don't want to owe money in 2039. Owning the practice outright by then means I can choose what it becomes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the farm as a safety net. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The farm has been in my family for four generations, and it's land, not a job. If medicine changes beyond recognition in 2039, I'd still have a stake in something real. My great-grandfather's fields will still need someone to own them when the robots arrive.

say: Ten years is **plenty of time** for the countryside to get this right.
Doctors who **prepare** will do well, and those who wait won't.
think: It's a **good decade**, with my practice open by about 2032.
My real worry is **getting comfortable** and not keeping up.

Open the practice around 2032 with a **loan repaid** before 2039.

feel: **Calm and hopeful**, with time to do things properly.
S4.quote: My great-grandfather's fields will still need someone to own them when the robots arrive.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, but more because of the rush than the AI. Two years means the big city companies grab the countryside before local doctors can get a practice open. What would help is cutting the red tape on opening small practices, and letting local doctors use the same AI tools as the big firms at a fair price.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how much the countryside is left out of these conversations. People talk about AI and jobs as if everyone lives in a city with a clinic on every corner. Out here in the valley, AI isn't taking a doctor's job, it's the only way some farms will ever have a doctor at all.

headlineQuote: Out here in the valley, AI isn't taking a doctor's job, it's the only way some farms will ever have a doctor at all.
portrait: Grace is a **27-year-old junior doctor** at Hollins Valley Health Centre, covering about forty farms and three villages.
She's single, lives on her **uncle's land** and saves hard, close to her farming family and church.

She stays **calm or uneasy** throughout, speeding up plans to open her own rural practice.
She blames **red tape** and city companies, and funds her plans through family and bank loans.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because city companies could grab the countryside before local doctors open practices.
whatWouldHelp: Less **red tape** for opening small practices.
Local doctors getting the **same AI tools** as big firms at a fair price.
